system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2134-01-19 19:41:00 to 2134-01-21 16:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease status post bypass, and diabetes was admitted after experiencing chest pain and bradycardia in the morning. He was found to have severe hyperkalemia (K 7.6), which was treated with intravenous calcium, insulin, and urgent hemodialysis. His chest pain and junctional rhythm resolved with potassium correction. Evaluation showed no evidence of acute myocardial infarction, with stable cardiac enzymes and a preserved ejection fraction on echocardiogram, though mild regional wall motion abnormality was noted. He had signs of mild volume overload on chest X-ray, consistent with acute on chronic diastolic heart failure. His lisinopril and metoprolol were held initially and restarted at discharge, with lisinopril dose increased to 5 mg daily. Sevelamer was doubled to help control potassium. He was discharged home after two days in stable condition with instructions to adhere to a low-potassium diet and attend all dialysis sessions.
problems: Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Diabetes with renal manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified

conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I had chest pain after my dialysis yesterday. It was sharp and got worse when I walked. I also felt nauseous and had diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did the pain go away at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the morphine in the ER helped. But I still felt weak and had muscle cramps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your EKG, and it shows some changes, but no signs of a heart attack. Your cardiac enzymes were negative, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t my heart? But I’ve had chest pain before with exertion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your typical chest pain is likely from heart disease, but this episode was different. It came with diarrhea and nausea, which makes us think it might be related to a viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But why did my blood pressure drop so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You became hypotensive after taking nitroglycerin in the ER. Also, the diarrhea may have left you a bit dehydrated, especially after dialysis. That likely contributed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I did feel lightheaded when I stood up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed that. It’s probably due to low blood volume. We’re giving you some fluids and holding your blood pressure meds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop them at home too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just for now. Once you're stable, we’ll restart them. Your blood pressure is already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about the chest pain when I press on my chest?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reproducible with touch, which suggests it’s from the chest wall, not your heart. It could be Tietze's disease—musculoskeletal inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not dangerous. We’ll treat it with ibuprofen. It should improve in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What tests did you do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray, which was stable—no pneumonia or fluid buildup. Your echo showed your heart is pumping okay, about 55% efficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My last echo was lower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s improved. There’s mild stiffness in the heart, which we see in diastolic heart failure, but it’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis is on track. We checked your labs—potassium is normal at 4.9, no infection signs. Blood cultures are negative too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time my potassium was high. I’m being careful with my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re increasing your sevelamer to help control potassium. Take three tablets with each meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No chest pain, and my stomach is settled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your diarrhea has stopped, and you’re not running a fever. We’ll resume your usual heart medications today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Including the aspirin and Plavix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both. And your beta-blocker, statin, and lisinopril. They’re important for your heart and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nitroglycerin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can keep using it if you have typical angina, but use it carefully—monitor your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I have dialysis today, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, scheduled for noon. We’ll make sure you go safely. Your blood pressure is stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back from dialysis? How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smooth. No issues. I feel lighter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ve recovered well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Any final instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your meds as prescribed, especially the new sevelamer dose. Watch for chest pain, dizziness, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel lightheaded?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stand up slowly. Use handgrip or foot dorsiflexion first. If it persists, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So no heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your tests ruled that out. The chest pain was atypical and likely from a viral illness and chest wall inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but stable. Continue your meds and dialysis. Follow up with your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes. Safe travels home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease, and diabetes was admitted with chest pain that began after dialysis. The pain was sharp, worse with exertion, and accompanied by nausea, diarrhea, and muscle cramps. Initial evaluation showed transient hypotension after nitroglycerin, EKG changes without cardiac enzyme elevation, and no evidence of acute myocardial infarction. The chest pain was determined to be atypical and likely related to a viral illness and chest wall inflammation, with improvement on ibuprofen. He also experienced lightheadedness, attributed to hypovolemia from recent illness and dialysis. His blood pressure stabilized, and cardiac medications were resumed. He underwent scheduled hemodialysis during admission and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue all medications, including an increased dose of sevelamer, and to follow up with his cardiologist.
problems: End stage renal disease on hemodialysis
